tasks.title: Statistics after ANALYZE
tasks.statement: Collect statistics with the ANALYZE command. The result is checked against the sqlite_stat1 table: it must contain index statistics rows.
tasks.hint: The ANALYZE; command is enough: SQLite will write the row count and the average number of rows per index value into sqlite_stat1.

tasks.title: Index for a filter
tasks.statement: The query SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7 scans the table. Create an index so that the plan becomes an index search.
tasks.hint: CREATE INDEX name ON orders (user_id);
tasks.starter:
-- index for WHERE user_id = ?
CREATE INDEX

tasks.title: Index on an expression
tasks.statement: The query SELECT * FROM users WHERE lower(email) = 'user5@mail.ru' does not use the index on email. Create an index on the expression lower(email) so that the plan becomes a search.
tasks.hint: CREATE INDEX … ON users (lower(email));
tasks.starter:
-- index on an expression
CREATE INDEX

tasks.title: Covering index
tasks.statement: The query SELECT created, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = 7 reads the table. Create one index that fully covers the query (the plan must contain COVERING INDEX).
tasks.hint: After user_id, add both needed columns to the index: created and total.

tasks.title: Column order in an index
tasks.statement: The query: WHERE status = 'new' AND user_id = 5. Create a composite index (columns in any order) so that the condition in the plan uses both columns: the plan text must contain `status=? AND user_id=?` or `user_id=? AND status=?`.
tasks.hint: Index (user_id, status): both conditions are equalities, both columns will take part in the search.

tasks.title: Index for a join
tasks.statement: The query SELECT u.email, o.total FROM users u JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.id WHERE u.id = 5 joins the tables. Create an index so that access to orders is an index search.
tasks.hint: Index the join column in the table where the search happens: orders.user_id.
tasks.starter:
-- index on a foreign key
CREATE INDEX

tasks.title: Selectivity of a condition
tasks.statement: Output the share of orders with status 'new' as a percentage with one decimal place: the column pct (ROUND to 1 digit).
tasks.hint: SUM(status = 'new') counts the matching rows, COUNT(*) counts all of them.

tasks.title: Number of distinct values
tasks.statement: For the columns city and status of the users table, output the number of distinct values: the columns cities, statuses.
tasks.hint: COUNT(DISTINCT …) for each column.

tasks.title: Most common values
tasks.statement: Output the most common values of city and the share of each as a percentage (integer): the columns city, pct; by descending share, then by city.
tasks.hint: GROUP BY city, COUNT(*), and the share of the total row count.

tasks.title: Histogram bucket bounds
tasks.statement: Split the orders into 4 equal-size buckets by total (NTILE) and output the largest total value in each bucket: the columns bucket, upper; ordered by bucket.
tasks.hint: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY total), then MAX(total) per bucket.

tasks.title: Estimate and actual
tasks.statement: The estimate under independence: the share of `city='Москва'` multiplied by the share of status='blocked' and by the number of rows. Output one row: est, the estimated number of rows (ROUND to an integer), and actual, the real number of rows where both conditions hold.
tasks.hint: est = n_city * n_status / n; actual is COUNT(*) with both conditions.

tasks.title: The NOT IN trap
tasks.statement: Output the ids from a that are not in b, so that a NULL in b does not break the result (NOT EXISTS): the column id; ascending.
tasks.hint: NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.id = a.id).

tasks.title: Pages without OFFSET
tasks.statement: Output the next page of 5 orders after the order with id 100, in ascending id order (without OFFSET): the columns id, total.
tasks.hint: WHERE id > 100 ORDER BY id LIMIT 5.

tasks.title: IN instead of a multiplying join
tasks.statement: Output the users (id, email) who have at least one order with status 'new', without duplicates. Use EXISTS. Ordered by id.
tasks.hint: EXISTS does not multiply rows, unlike JOIN.

tasks.title: Join size
tasks.statement: Output the number of rows in the result of joining users and orders on user_id: the column n.
tasks.hint: Each order finds its user, so the result equals the number of orders.

tasks.title: Cost of a scan
tasks.statement: The cost of a sequential scan = pages · 1.0 + rows · 0.01. Write seq_scan_cost(pages, rows): a number rounded to two decimal places.
tasks.hint: Plug into the formula and round.

tasks.title: Cost of an index lookup
tasks.statement: Index lookup: for each matching row, a random page read (4.0) plus 0.01 per row, plus the descent through the tree (height · 4.0). Write index_scan_cost(matching_rows, height): a number rounded to two decimal places.
tasks.hint: height·4 + rows·(4 + 0.01).

tasks.title: Scan or index?
tasks.statement: A scan costs pages + rows·0.01, an index costs height·4 + matching·4.01. Write choose_access(pages, rows, matching, height): `seq` if the scan is strictly cheaper, otherwise `index`. The function returns the strings 'seq' and 'index'.
tasks.hint: Compare the two costs; on a tie we choose the index.

tasks.title: Break-even point
tasks.statement: For a scan costing pages + rows·0.01 and an index costing height·4 + m·4.01, find the largest integer number of matching rows m for which the index is still no more expensive than the scan. Write breakeven_rows(pages, rows, height); if even at m = 0 the index is more expensive, return −1.
tasks.hint: m = (seq − height·4) / 4.01, round down and check the boundary.

tasks.title: Nested loops
tasks.statement: The outer table returns outer_rows rows. For each one a lookup in the inner table is made: index_probe_cost if there is an index, otherwise a scan of inner_pages. Write nested_loop_cost(outer_rows, inner_pages, has_index, index_probe_cost): outer_rows · (index_probe_cost if has_index, otherwise inner_pages).
tasks.hint: Multiply the number of outer rows by the price of one lookup.

tasks.title: Hash join
tasks.statement: A hash join reads both tables once and builds a hash table on the smaller one: cost = pages_a + pages_b + 0.02·(rows_a + rows_b). Write hash_join_cost(pages_a, rows_a, pages_b, rows_b): a number rounded to two decimal places.
tasks.hint: Add the pages and 0.02 of the sum of rows.

tasks.title: Merge join
tasks.statement: A merge needs sorting for each unsorted side: n·log₂(n)·0.01 (round the total to two decimal places; for n ≤ 1 sorting costs 0), then a pass of 0.01·(rows_a + rows_b). Write merge_join_cost(rows_a, sorted_a, rows_b, sorted_b): sorted_* = True means no sort is needed.
tasks.hint: A per-side sort function + a linear pass.

tasks.title: Choosing a join algorithm
tasks.statement: Write pick_join(outer_rows, inner_has_index, equality, both_sorted): if the join is not on equality, `nested`; otherwise if both sides are sorted, `merge`; otherwise if the inner table has an index and outer_rows ≤ 100, `nested`; otherwise `hash`. The function returns the strings 'nested', 'merge', 'hash'.
tasks.hint: Check the conditions in the given order.

tasks.title: Equality selectivity
tasks.statement: Column statistics: mcv is a dictionary "value → fraction" (the most common ones), n_distinct is the number of distinct values. For a value from mcv the selectivity is its fraction; otherwise the remaining fraction (1 − the sum of the mcv fractions) is divided equally among the other distinct values: (1 − Σ) / (n_distinct − len(mcv)). Write eq_selectivity(mcv, n_distinct, value): a number rounded to 4 decimal places.
tasks.hint: Two cases: the value is among the common ones, or in the tail.

tasks.title: Range selectivity
tasks.statement: The histogram is a list of bucket bounds, bounds (increasing), with an equal number of rows in each bucket. The fraction of rows in the range [lo, hi] is the number of buckets lying entirely inside plus the parts of the edge buckets (linear interpolation), divided by the number of buckets. Write range_selectivity(bounds, lo, hi): a number rounded to 4 decimal places; a range outside the bounds is clipped.
tasks.hint: For each bucket take the fraction of its length that falls into the range; add them up and divide by the number of buckets.

tasks.title: Row count estimate
tasks.statement: A table of rows rows, a list of condition selectivities sels, the conditions are independent. Write combined_rows(rows, sels): the estimated number of rows, rows · the product of the fractions, rounded to an integer but not less than 1.
tasks.hint: Multiply the fractions and multiply by the number of rows; minimum 1.

tasks.title: Join size
tasks.statement: Estimate of the size of an equality join: |A|·|B| / max(d_a, d_b), where d_* is the number of distinct key values in the table. Write join_cardinality(rows_a, rows_b, d_a, d_b): the estimate rounded to an integer (minimum 0).
tasks.hint: Put the formula into code; divide by the maximum of the distinct counts.

tasks.title: Estimation error
tasks.statement: Q-error is how many times the estimate differs from the actual value: max(est/actual, actual/est), rounded to two decimal places. Write q_error(est, actual); if either value is 0, replace it with 1.
tasks.hint: Replace zeros with 1, then take the maximum of the two ratios.

tasks.title: How many join orders
tasks.statement: For n tables the number of left-deep join orders is n!, and the number of all orders including tree shapes (bushy) is (2n−2)! / (n−1)!. Write join_orders(n): a pair [left-deep, all]. For n = 1 it is [1, 1].
tasks.hint: math.factorial; for n = 1 return ones.

tasks.title: Best join order
tasks.statement: Given the table sizes sizes and a common join selectivity sel (the same for all pairs): the size of the join of a subset of size k is the product of the sizes · sel^(k−1). A left-deep order costs the sum of the sizes of all intermediate results (after each join). Write best_order_cost(sizes, sel): the minimum cost, rounded to two decimal places (for a single table, 0).
tasks.hint: Go through the permutations and compute the sum of the intermediate results; take the minimum.

tasks.title: The most expensive node
tasks.statement: A plan is a list of nodes [depth, name, total cost] in output order (a parent comes before its children; the root has depth 0). A node's own cost = its total minus the sum of the total costs of its direct children. Write hottest_node(plan): the name of the node with the largest own cost (on a tie, the first in order).
tasks.hint: For each node subtract the total costs of its direct children: these are the following nodes with depth one greater, until you return to the same or a smaller depth.

tasks.title: The heaviest queries
tasks.statement: The statistics are a list of [query, calls, average time in ms]. Total time = calls · average. Write top_total_time(stats, k): a list of the names of the k heaviest queries by total time (descending; on a tie, by name).
tasks.hint: Sort by descending calls·average and then by name.

tasks.title: Generic or custom plan
tasks.statement: The costs of the custom plans of the first calls are the list custom. The generic plan costs generic. The rule: use the generic plan if generic ≤ the average of the custom ones · 1.1 and there were at least 5 calls; otherwise a custom one. Write use_generic_plan(custom, generic): True if we choose the generic one.
tasks.hint: First check the number of calls, then compare with the average.
